MiniGames.title: Mini-game worlds
MiniGames.intro: Meet the chess pieces! Each world teaches one piece with little games. Collect stars — there's no losing, just try again.
MiniGames.goalStarSafe: Reach the star — but don't stop on a red square!
MiniGames.caught: Oops! A black piece captured you on that square.
MiniGames.wellDone: Well done! Can you do it in fewer moves?
MiniGames.pawnWarsGoal: Pawn wars! Get a pawn to the other side first.
MiniGames.pawnWarsLost: The computer's pawn got there first. Try again!
MiniGames.noPuzzles: No puzzles found for this level yet.
MiniGames.loadError: Something went wrong. Please try again.
MiniGames.rookStory: Hi, I'm Rosie the Rook! I walk in straight lines — up, down, left and right — as far as I like. I can't jump over other pieces!
MiniGames.bishopStory: I'm Bob the Bishop. I slide on diagonals and I always stay on squares of the same colour. Can you find my path?
MiniGames.queenStory: I'm Queen Quinn, the strongest piece! I move like a rook AND like a bishop. Use my power wisely!
MiniGames.kingStory: I'm King Shaky. I'm a bit scared, so I take one small step at a time — in any direction.
MiniGames.knightStory: Neigh! I'm Kip the Knight. I jump in an L: two squares one way, then one to the side. I can jump over other pieces, but cannot land on one of my own!
MiniGames.pawnStory: I'm Pip the Pawn. I walk straight forward (two steps on my first move!) but I capture diagonally. Reach the end and I become a queen!
MiniGames.captureStory: Welcome to Capture Island! Take the black pieces — and watch out: never stop on a square a black piece is guarding (the red squares).
MiniGames.mateStory: This is Checkmate Castle. Checkmate means the king is attacked and can't escape. Find the move that traps him!
MiniGames.friendlyPawns: Move only the highlighted {piece}. The other white pawns stay in place and block your path.
MiniGames.friendlyPawnsKnight: Move only the highlighted {piece}. The white pawns stay in place. You can jump over them, but cannot land on them.

Levels.title: Levels: from Pawn to King
Levels.intro: Piece names mark your rank. Each level teaches a tactic and has {count} exercises. Solve {pass} without mistakes or help to move up. Tests do not change your rating; you can retry any time.
Levels.passed: Level passed! {correct} of {count} solved without help. 🎉
Levels.notYet: {correct} solved without help — you need {need}. Practise and try again!
Levels.noPuzzles: There is not yet a full set of exercises for this topic and difficulty. Please practise the lesson and try again later.
Levels.lesson_pawn-1: Begin with safe captures of undefended pieces. Look at which enemy piece is unprotected, then find a piece that can take it safely. The test uses small positions and one-move captures.
Levels.lesson_pawn-2: Checkmate means the king is attacked and has no escape. Look for checks first — which one leaves the king nowhere to go?
Levels.lesson_pawn-3: Mix it up: sometimes there's a checkmate, sometimes a free piece. Always look for checks and captures first.
Levels.lesson_knight-1: A fork attacks two pieces at once. Knights are the best at forks — look for a jump that hits the king and another piece!
Levels.lesson_knight-2: The knight can give checkmate too, often when the king is boxed in by its own pieces. A knight check cannot be blocked, so look for a jump that checks a king with no free squares. In every puzzle here the knight gives the final blow.
Levels.lesson_knight-3: Forks and free pieces. Before you move, ask: can I attack two things at once?
Levels.lesson_bishop-1: A pin means a piece can't move because something more valuable is behind it. Bishops love to pin!
Levels.lesson_bishop-2: A skewer is a pin in reverse: attack the big piece first, and when it moves, take what's behind it.
Levels.lesson_bishop-3: Checkmate in two: the first move forces the opponent, the second one is mate. Look for a forcing check or capture.
Levels.lesson_rook-1: Back-rank mate: when the king is stuck behind its own pawns, a rook or queen on the back rank is checkmate!
Levels.lesson_rook-2: Discovered attack: move one piece out of the way and the piece behind it attacks. Two threats at once!
Levels.lesson_rook-3: Endgames with rooks, and races to make a new queen. Put your rook behind passed pawns, keep your king active, and look for the moment a pawn can safely promote.
Levels.lesson_queen-1: Deflection: lure a defender away from its job, then strike what it was protecting.
Levels.lesson_queen-2: Attraction: sacrifice to pull the king or a piece onto a bad square, then finish the attack.
Levels.lesson_queen-3: Sometimes the strongest move gives away the queen! Look for queen sacrifices that lead to mate or win back more, and for captures that remove the piece defending the opponent's position.
Levels.lesson_king-1: You've reached King! Each King test is a little harder. How far can you climb?

LevelExercises.captureExplanation: The {piece} moves from {from} to {to} and captures the undefended {target}. No enemy piece can recapture it there.
LevelExercises.goal_hangingPiece: Capture an undefended enemy piece without losing your own piece.
LevelExercises.explain_hangingPiece: Check which enemy pieces are unprotected. Capture one safely: an enemy piece must not be able to take your capturing piece afterwards.
LevelExercises.goal_mateIn1: Checkmate the enemy king in one move.
LevelExercises.explain_mateIn1: Find a check that the king cannot escape. The opponent must be unable to move away, block the check, or capture the checking piece.
LevelExercises.goal_mateIn2: Force checkmate in two of your moves.
LevelExercises.explain_mateIn2: Start with a forcing move. After the opponent’s reply, find a check that leaves the king no escape.
LevelExercises.goal_fork: Create a fork: attack two enemy pieces at once.
LevelExercises.explain_fork: A fork creates two threats with one move. The opponent usually cannot protect both targets, so you can win material.
LevelExercises.goal_pin: Use a pin to win material or strengthen your attack.
LevelExercises.explain_pin: A pinned piece cannot move safely because a king or a more valuable piece is behind it. Attack or exploit that pinned piece.
LevelExercises.goal_skewer: Use a skewer to win the piece behind a more valuable target.
LevelExercises.explain_skewer: Attack the more valuable piece first. When it moves away, capture the piece that was hidden behind it.
LevelExercises.goal_backRankMate: Checkmate the king on its back rank.
LevelExercises.explain_backRankMate: Look for a rook or queen check along the back rank. The king’s own pawns can block its escape squares.
LevelExercises.goal_discoveredAttack: Move a blocking piece to reveal a strong attack.
LevelExercises.explain_discoveredAttack: Moving one piece can open a line for a bishop, rook, or queen. Look for a move that creates a second threat while uncovering the attack.
LevelExercises.goal_endgame: Find the best continuation in this endgame.
LevelExercises.explain_endgame: In an endgame, an active king and advancing pawns are often decisive. Check threats, safe king moves, and promotion opportunities.
LevelExercises.goal_deflection: Draw a defender away, then exploit what it was protecting.
LevelExercises.explain_deflection: A defender may have to protect a vital square or piece. Force it away so that your next threat succeeds.
LevelExercises.goal_attraction: Force an enemy piece onto a vulnerable square.
LevelExercises.explain_attraction: An attraction tactic lures a piece or king to a square where a follow-up check, capture, or fork becomes possible.
LevelExercises.explain_tactics: Look at checks, captures, and direct threats first. Follow the opponent’s reply and work out how to finish your idea.
LevelExercises.solutionInstructions: Follow the blue arrow and play each solution move with the button below.
LevelExercises.reviewInstructions: Review the move and explanation, then try again or continue.
LevelExercises.retryInstructions: Read the feedback, then retry this exercise or review its solution.
LevelExercises.goal_knightMate: Checkmate the king; the knight gives the final blow.
LevelExercises.explain_knightMate: A knight check cannot be blocked. When the king's escape squares are taken by its own pieces or yours, a knight jump can be checkmate.
LevelExercises.goal_rookEndgame: Find the best move in this rook endgame.
LevelExercises.explain_rookEndgame: In rook endgames, active rooks and passed pawns decide. Look for checks, attacks on loose pawns, and ways to push or stop a pawn.
LevelExercises.goal_promotion: Get a pawn to the last rank and make a new queen.
LevelExercises.explain_promotion: Check whether your pawn can reach the last square safely. Sometimes you first need to block, deflect or chase away the piece that stops it.
LevelExercises.goal_queenSacrifice: Give up your queen to win the game or win back more.
LevelExercises.explain_queenSacrifice: A queen sacrifice works when the reply is forced: after the opponent takes the queen, you mate or win even more material.
LevelExercises.goal_sacrifice: Sacrifice material to win more or to attack the king.
LevelExercises.explain_sacrifice: A sacrifice gives something away on purpose. Check what the opponent must do after taking it, and what you win then.
LevelExercises.goal_capturingDefender: Capture the piece that defends something important.
LevelExercises.explain_capturingDefender: Find which enemy piece guards a key square or piece. Take that defender, and what it was protecting falls.

safeCapture.title: Take an undefended piece
safeCapture.intro: The rook moves in straight lines. The black knight on a5 has no defender. Can the rook capture it safely?
safeCapture.example: The rook took the knight. The black king is too far away to take the rook back.
safeCapture.find: Tap a5, where the captured knight stood.
safeCapture.challenge: A fresh position! Use the rook to capture the undefended bishop.
safeCapture.takeaway: Before capturing, look for the opponent’s possible recapture.

checkmate.title: Check or checkmate?
checkmate.intro: Checkmate is check with no escape. The queen and king can work together to trap the other king.
checkmate.example: The queen gives check on g7. Our king protects the queen and the black king has no safe escape.
checkmate.find: Tap the black king that is checkmated.
checkmate.challenge: The queen starts on a different square. Give checkmate in one move.
checkmate.takeaway: For checkmate, check the attack, every escape square, and whether the checking piece can be captured.

fork.title: Two targets, one knight
fork.intro: A fork attacks two pieces at once. Watch the knight jump to f7.
fork.example: The knight attacks the king on h8 AND the queen on d8. The king must answer the check first.
fork.find: Tap both pieces attacked by the knight.
fork.challenge: A new fork! Jump the knight to e7 to attack the king and queen together.
fork.takeaway: Look for a square where your knight attacks two valuable targets.

pin.title: A piece that cannot move
pin.intro: Watch the bishop move to b5 and line up with the knight and king.
pin.example: The knight on d7 is pinned to its king on e8. Moving the knight would expose the king to check, so it cannot legally move.
pin.find: Tap the pinned knight and the king behind it.
pin.challenge: Create the same pin from a new square. Move the bishop to b5.
pin.takeaway: A piece pinned to its king cannot move if that would expose the king.

defend.title: Notice the opponent’s threat
defend.intro: The black rook on a8 attacks our rook down the open a-file. We can move our rook to safety.
defend.example: Our rook moves off the attacked file. First notice the danger, then choose a safe square.
defend.find: Tap the black rook that was making the threat.
defend.challenge: The black rook now attacks our rook on the c-file. Move our rook to a safe square.
defend.takeaway: After the opponent moves, ask: what is attacked, and how can I keep it safe?

Endgames.title: Finish the endgame
Endgames.intro: First learn the strategy with an annotated board tutorial. Then try a random endgame on your own. You can return to the tutorial without losing your practice position.
Endgames.engineError: The endgame advisor could not reply. Try again shortly, or take back your move.
Endgames.restart: Start again from a new position
Endgames.stalemateHelp: The king is not in check and has no legal move. That is a draw, not checkmate. Restart and leave an escape square until you are ready to give mate.
Endgames.wonAlone: You reached the goal without hints, takebacks or returning to the tutorial during this attempt.
Endgames.wonWithHelp: You reached the goal with help. Try a new position when you feel ready.
Endgames.tryAgainHelp: A tricky ending is a chance to learn. Replay the example and try again.

queenMate.title: King and queen mate
queenMate.instruction: You are White. Use your queen and king together to give checkmate. Keep an eye on stalemate.
queenMate.demo: The white king protects the queen on g7. The queen checks the black king and covers its escape squares.

rookMate.title: King and rook mate
rookMate.instruction: You are White. Bring your king closer and use the rook to give checkmate at the edge.
rookMate.demo: The king on g6 guards g7 and h7. The rook moves to a8 to check along the last rank.

promotion.title: Promote a pawn
promotion.instruction: You are White. Help your pawn reach the last rank. Keep the king close enough to protect its journey.
promotion.demo: A pawn on the seventh rank needs one more safe step. Here it can promote on f8.

opposition.title: King and pawn teamwork
opposition.instruction: You are White. Use your king to make space for the pawn and promote it. The defending king will try to block you.
opposition.demo: One winning example: the king makes space, the pawn advances, and the king protects the promotion route. Your opponent may choose different replies in practice.

holdDraw.title: Save a rook-pawn ending
holdDraw.instruction: You are White with only a king. Stay near the pawn’s promotion corner and try to reach a draw. Sometimes taking the pawn is possible too.
holdDraw.demo: If Black moves the king to g3 here, White has no legal move but is not in check. This is stalemate: a draw.

Endgames.verifiedStarts: Random legal starts and endgame moves verified with tablebases

bishopPairMate.title: King and two bishops mate
bishopPairMate.instruction: You are White. Your bishops cover opposite-colored squares. Bring your king up and squeeze the opposing king toward an edge, then a corner. Keep both bishops safe.
bishopPairMate.demo: The king protects g7 and covers g8. One bishop covers h7; the other gives check on g7. The pieces cover every escape together.

bishopKnightMate.title: King, bishop and knight mate
bishopKnightMate.instruction: You are White. Work with all three pieces. Drive the king toward a corner of the same color as your bishop. The knight covers squares your bishop cannot reach. This is an advanced challenge.
bishopKnightMate.demo: The knight on f6 covers g8 and h7. The king protects g7, and the bishop moves to g7 to deliver mate in the correct-colored corner.

Defense.title: Defense detective
Defense.intro: Ten detective levels. Start with simple attacks in Level 1, then tackle increasingly difficult defensive puzzles from our collection in Levels 2–10. Each round has five untimed positions.

Defense.identify: Which white piece is in danger?

Defense.wrongPiece: Look again: which white piece can Black take?
Defense.wrongMove: That move leaves trouble. Watch a possible reply, then choose another defense.

EndgameLessons.legend: Blue squares show the idea. Gold squares and the arrow show the last example move.
EndgameLessons.examples: These are short teaching examples, not one sequence to memorize. The defending king can choose other moves in your random practice position.

queenMate.check1: Use the queen to make the king’s space smaller; do not chase with endless checks.
queenMate.check2: Bring your king up while keeping the queen safe.
queenMate.check3: At the edge, cover escapes and give check. No check plus no legal move is stalemate.
queenMate.trap: A queen can cover every escape too soon. Before a quiet queen move, check whether the opponent will still have a legal move.

fence.title: Build a fence with the queen
fence.explain: The black king is on f6. The queen can form a fence across a file and a rank. Watch Qe4: the king cannot cross the e-file or the fourth rank while the queen controls them.
fence.after: After Qe4 and …Kg7, the king stays above the fourth rank and to the right of the e-file. Aim to tighten this space gradually while your king approaches.

king.title: The queen needs its king
king.explain: Our king is on f4 and the defending king is on h7. Rather than giving another check, bring our king toward the area we have restricted.
king.after: Kg5 gives our king a more active post. After …Kh8, we still need to coordinate both pieces; the queen should not have to do everything alone.

stalemate.title: Spot the stalemate trap
stalemate.explain: This is a deliberately bad example. With our king on g6 and Black on h8, Qf7 would cover all three neighbouring squares without checking the king. Watch what happens.
stalemate.after: Qf7 is stalemate: h8 is not attacked, but g8, g7 and h7 are unavailable. That is a draw. Leave an escape until you can give a real mating check.

mate.title: Finish with a protected check
mate.explain: Here the queen starts on f7 and our king on g6. The king protects g7. Put the queen where it gives check and closes the remaining exits.
mate.after: Qg7# checks h8. The queen covers g8 and h7, and our king protects the queen on g7. Every escape and capture has been answered.

rookMate.check1: Use a rook file or rank as a wall, and keep the rook out of reach.
rookMate.check2: Bring your king up to take away escape squares.
rookMate.check3: Use a waiting move if needed; give the final rank/file check only when the king covers the exits.
rookMate.trap: Random checks let the king wander. A rook wall plus an active king is more useful than checking on every turn. Do not leave the rook next to the enemy king unprotected.

fence.title: Cut the board with a rook wall
fence.explain: The black king is on f6. Re1 puts a wall on the e-file. The rook controls the highlighted squares, so the king cannot cross that file.
fence.after: After Re1 and …Kf7, the wall remains. Keep the rook safe and use your king to help reduce the space on the other side.

king.title: Advance the king behind the wall
king.explain: Our rook already controls the e-file. The king can move from c3 to d4, taking a more active position without dismantling the rook wall.
king.after: The king on d4 helps control central squares such as e5. Continue improving the king’s position while the rook keeps the defender confined.

wait.title: A quiet move can make the king move
wait.explain: Black is on h8. Our king on f6 and rook on a7 cover g7 and h7, leaving g8. A rook move along the seventh rank can keep those restrictions without giving check.
wait.after: Rb7 is a waiting move. Black must play …Kg8 in this example. You changed whose turn it was without losing the wall.

mate.title: King and rook close the last exits
mate.explain: The defending king is on h8 and our king is on g6. Our king covers g7 and h7. The rook can now give the final check along the back rank.
mate.after: Ra8# checks along the eighth rank. The rook controls g8, and our king covers g7 and h7. That cooperation makes it mate.

promotion.check1: Bring the king ahead of the pawn toward useful key squares.
promotion.check2: Before every push, check whether the enemy king can take the pawn.
promotion.check3: Escort the pawn to the last rank; do not abandon its protection just to move faster.
promotion.trap: Being closer to the pawn is only a starting advantage. An unprotected push can still lose it. Check the defending king’s next move before advancing.

lead.title: Let the king lead the way
lead.explain: The pawn is on e3. For this non-rook pawn, d5, e5 and f5 are key squares. Watch the king step onto e5, ahead of the pawn.
lead.after: Ke5 gives the pawn an escort in front. After …Kb7, the king holds an important square while the pawn prepares to follow.

protect.title: Push when the king can protect the pawn
protect.explain: With the king on e5, the pawn can step from e3 to e4 and remain next to its king. Compare this with sending a pawn forward alone.
protect.after: After e4, our king on e5 protects the pawn on e4. Keep asking whether the next square will be safe before each new push.

rush.title: A rushed pawn can be captured
rush.explain: This is a deliberately bad push. Our king on f2 is too far away to protect e5. If the pawn runs from e4 to e5, Black can take it.
rush.after: After e5? …Kxe5, the pawn is gone and only two kings remain. Advance the king when the pawn would otherwise be left unprotected.

promote.title: Take the final safe step
promote.explain: The pawn is on f7, our king is on f6, and the defending king is far away on h8. The pawn can now reach the last rank.
promote.after: f8=Q+ promotes safely. In a real game you would continue toward checkmate; in this challenge, reaching promotion completes the goal.

opposition.check1: Identify who must move when the kings face each other across one empty square.
opposition.check2: Use a king move to go around the defender when it steps aside.
opposition.check3: Push the pawn only when your king can protect its route and promotion square.
opposition.trap: Opposition is a tool, not a rule to follow blindly. Do not make a pawn push automatically when a king move can win access to a useful square.

face.title: Understand whose turn matters
face.explain: The kings on e6 and e8 face each other across the empty e7-square. Here it is Black’s turn. Black must move its king away from this face-to-face position.
face.after: After …Kd8, Kf7 goes around the defender. The king on f7 controls e8 and helps clear a route for the pawn.

side.title: Go around the defending king
side.explain: In this example White moves first. Kf6 goes to the side. After the sample reply …Kf8, the pawn can advance under the king’s protection.
side.after: Kf6 …Kf8 e6 is one useful continuation. Black can defend differently in your game, so look for the same ideas rather than copying the moves.

escort.title: Keep the pawn protected as the king changes sides
escort.explain: The pawn on e6 can move to e7, protected by our king on f6. When Black steps to d7, our king can move to f7.
escort.after: After e7 …Kd7 Kf7, our king protects e8. Black cannot simply step onto that promotion square to block the pawn.

promote.title: Use the route your king created
promote.explain: Our king on f7 guards e8 and the pawn is on e7. Watch one legal defending reply and the final promotion.
promote.after: After …Kd6, e8=Q completes the promotion. The king’s work created the safe route; the pawn did not need to race ahead alone.

holdDraw.check1: Find the rook-pawn’s promotion corner: h1 for a black h-pawn, a1 for a black a-pawn.
holdDraw.check2: Keep your king close to that corner and avoid being driven away.
holdDraw.check3: Recognize stalemate, or capture the pawn if the square is genuinely safe.
holdDraw.trap: Do not run far from the promotion corner, and do not assume every pawn can be captured. The opposing king may protect it.

corner.title: Head for the promotion corner
corner.explain: Black’s h-pawn wants to reach h1. Our king on f2 can approach through g1. The corner is a useful shelter when the attacking king cannot drive us away.
corner.after: Kg1 …Kg4 Kh1 reaches the corner in this example. Stay alert to checks and keep access to this shelter.

stalemate.title: Understand why the corner can save a draw
stalemate.explain: Our king is on h1, Black’s king is on g3, and the pawn is on h3. If Black pushes to h2, all of our exits disappear — but h1 is not in check.
stalemate.after: …h2 is stalemate. The pawn controls g1 and the black king controls g2 and h2. White has no legal move and is not in check, so the game is drawn.

capture.title: Take an unprotected pawn when it is safe
capture.explain: This time Black’s king is on g4, which does not control h2. Our king on h1 is allowed to capture the pawn on h2.
capture.after: Kxh2 leaves only two kings, so the game is drawn. The important check was whether the opposing king protected the capture square.

bishopPairMate.check1: Use the bishops together: each covers one colour of squares.
bishopPairMate.check2: Bring the king up while the bishops build diagonal barriers.
bishopPairMate.check3: Drive the king to an edge and build a mating net, checking every escape before the final check.
bishopPairMate.trap: Two bishops still need their king. Do not separate the pieces carelessly, lose a bishop to the defending king, or cover every escape without giving check.

diagonals.title: Build a net on both colours
diagonals.explain: The bishops work on different colours. After Bf4, one bishop controls e4, f5 and g6; the other controls g5 and h6. These diagonal barriers work together.
diagonals.after: After Bf4 …Ke6, look at the two sets of diagonal squares. Use the pair to restrict routes, rather than chasing the king with one bishop alone.

king.title: The king completes the bishop barriers
king.explain: Our king on d4 can move to e5 while the bishops stay coordinated. The king is needed to cover squares that the diagonals alone leave open.
king.after: After Ke5 …Kg8, our king has an active role and controls squares such as d6, e6 and f6. Keep the pieces cooperating as the defender approaches an edge.

net.title: See how the pieces share the last squares
net.explain: In this finishing example, our king on f7 covers g8 and protects g7. The bishop on f5 covers h7. The bishop on h6 can give the mating check.
net.after: Bg7# checks the king on h8. One bishop gives check, the other closes h7, and the king supports the net. Every piece has a job.

bishopKnightMate.check1: Aim for a corner of the same colour as your bishop.
bishopKnightMate.check2: Use the king as a wall, and coordinate the knight with the bishop to cover both colours.
bishopKnightMate.check3: Recognize useful knight routes, but recalculate the king’s escapes after every reply.
bishopKnightMate.trap: The knight route is not an automatic recipe. Check every enemy capture and escape after each move. Keep the knight and bishop safe while aiming for a corner of the bishop’s colour.

corner.title: Choose the right-coloured corner
corner.explain: The bishop on b3 runs on light squares and protects our knight on f7 along b3–c4–d5–e6–f7. The matching mating corners are a8 and h1, highlighted in blue.
corner.after: The bishop’s colour determines the target corners. In a different starting position, a dark-squared bishop would point you toward a1 or h8.

wall.title: Make a wall with the king
wall.explain: Our king can move from c6 to d6 to control c7, d7 and e7. The bishop on b3 protects the knight on f7: Black cannot play …Kxf7 because f7 is attacked by the bishop.
wall.after: After Kd6 …Kf8, c7, d7 and e7 remain controlled by our king, and the bishop still protects f7. Always check the defender’s captures before moving your king away from a piece.

routeA.title: Recognize the first half of a knight route
routeA.explain: A useful pattern is a W-shaped knight route. The bishop on b3 protects the starting square f7. Follow f7–e5–d7 with example king replies; e5 is out of the black king’s reach, and our king on c6 protects d7.
routeA.after: After Ne5 …Ke8 Nd7 …Kd8, the knight is on d7, supported by the king. This illustrates a pattern, not a claim that Black must choose these exact replies.

routeB.title: Continue the pattern toward the corner
routeB.explain: Continue the example route d7–c5–b7. Notice how our king supports these knight posts while the defending king moves toward the a8 side.
routeB.after: After Nc5 …Kc8 Nb7 …Kb8, the route f7–e5–d7–c5–b7 is complete. Further king and bishop coordination is still needed to finish; the W alone is not checkmate.

mate.title: Finish by sharing the escape squares
mate.explain: This final example has a dark-squared bishop, so h8 is the right-coloured corner. The knight on f6 controls g8 and h7, and our king protects g7.
mate.after: Bg7# gives the final check on h8. The knight closes g8 and h7, the king protects g7, and the bishop supplies the check.

EndgameHints.focus: Blue squares mark strategic targets; they are not all legal moves right now.
EndgameHints.cannotWin: With accurate defense, this position no longer forces the winning goal. You can practise the best resistance or take back a move to restore your chance.
EndgameHints.cannotDraw: The defender can now force a win with accurate play. Practise resisting, or take back a move to return to a drawable position.
EndgameHints.plan_fence: The defending king is on {enemyKing}. Use the piece on {heavy} to fence off space, then bring your king on {king} up behind the fence.
EndgameHints.plan_edge: The defending king is already at the edge on {enemyKing}. Coordinate your king on {king} with the mating piece; close the exits before the final check, and watch for stalemate.
EndgameHints.plan_pawn: Your pawn is on {pawn}, and your king is on {king}. The useful key squares are {keys}. Use the king to control the route before pushing the pawn past its protection.
EndgameHints.plan_rookPawn: Your pawn is on the edge at {pawn}. Rook pawns have different winning rules: focus on the promotion corner {corner}, not the usual three key squares.
EndgameHints.plan_corner: The black pawn on {pawn} wants to promote on {corner}. Your king on {king} should keep access to that corner and avoid being driven away from it.
EndgameHints.plan_survive: The pawn has already promoted. Your king is on {king}; survival is harder now. Consider taking back a move to practise the original drawing method.
EndgameHints.plan_finish: The king on {enemyKing} can be checkmated on this move. Look for a checking move that leaves no escape, capture or block.
EndgameHints.plan_promoteNow: Your pawn on {pawn} can reach the last rank on this move. Look at the promotion square and finish the challenge’s goal.
EndgameHints.plan_takePawn: The pawn on {pawn} is within reach of your king on {king}, and a legal capture is available. Taking the last pawn will leave a draw with two kings.
EndgameHints.plan_inCheck: Your king on {king} is in check. First find a legal escape or capture; a longer-term plan cannot ignore the current check.
EndgameHints.plan_bishops: The king on {enemyKing} currently has {before} legal king moves. Use both bishop colours as diagonal barriers and bring your king on {king} into the net.
EndgameHints.plan_bishopKnight: Your bishop on {bishop} controls {color}, so the target corners are {corners}. Coordinate the king on {king} and knight to guide the king from {enemyKing} toward a matching corner.
EndgameHints.plan_bishopKnightCorner: The defending king is already in the right-coloured corner on {enemyKing}. Keep it confined while your king on {king} and knight close the remaining exits; your bishop on {bishop} can then help finish the mating net. Do not let the king slip back into open space.
EndgameHints.reason_mate: Look for the final check. Confirm that the opponent cannot move its king, capture the checking piece or block the check.
EndgameHints.reason_stalemate: The suggested move reaches stalemate. That saves a draw, but would not complete a checkmate challenge.
EndgameHints.reason_drawCapture: The suggested king move captures the last pawn safely. Only two kings will remain.
EndgameHints.reason_promotion: The pawn can reach the last rank now. Check the promotion square rather than moving the king again automatically.
EndgameHints.reason_reachCorner: The suggested king move reaches the pawn’s promotion corner. Use that shelter to resist promotion.
EndgameHints.reason_approachCorner: This king move reduces the distance to the pawn’s promotion corner. Stay on the route to that shelter.
EndgameHints.reason_holdCorner: This king move is the tablebase’s best defense. Keep watching the promotion corner and whether the pawn can be captured safely.
EndgameHints.reason_supportedPawn: This push keeps the pawn on a square guarded by your king. The king and pawn can advance as a team.
EndgameHints.reason_pawnStep: The pawn moves in the suggested plan. Compare its next square with the defending king’s reach; not every useful push is beside your king.
EndgameHints.reason_keySquare: The suggested king move occupies one of this pawn’s key squares. Win control of space before asking the pawn to move again.
EndgameHints.reason_opposition: This king move places the kings across one empty square from each other. Black must move its king next; use that change of turn to make progress.
EndgameHints.reason_kingApproach: This king move really brings your king closer to the defending king. Active king support helps close the net or escort the pawn.
EndgameHints.reason_kingWall: This king move is about controlling space, not necessarily getting closer. Think of the squares the king will take away.
EndgameHints.reason_knight: The knight supplies a different set of controlled squares. Look for a post that works with the bishop and king, not just a checking jump.
EndgameHints.reason_bishop: Use the bishop’s diagonal as part of the net. Keep the other pieces involved so the king cannot simply escape on the other colour.
EndgameHints.reason_restrict: This move reduces the opponent’s legal king moves from {before} to {after}. That is a concrete way to make the net tighter.
EndgameHints.reason_checkFence: This is a checking move with the mating piece. Check how your king and piece cover the remaining routes; a check alone is not the whole plan.
EndgameHints.reason_keepFence: This move repositions the mating piece without requiring a smaller number of king moves immediately. Keep the wall and king support working together.
EndgameHints.effect_mate: After {move}, the king on {enemyKing} is in check and has no legal reply: checkmate.
EndgameHints.effect_stalemate: After {move}, Black is not in check and has no legal move. This is a draw, not mate.
EndgameHints.effect_drawCapture: After {move}, the pawn is gone and the two kings cannot checkmate each other: a draw.
EndgameHints.effect_promotion: After {move}, the pawn has promoted on {to}. You have reached this challenge’s goal.
EndgameHints.effect_reachCorner: After {move}, your king reaches {to}, the pawn’s promotion corner.
EndgameHints.effect_approachCorner: After {move}, your king is on {to}, nearer to {corner}. Recheck the attacking king’s reply before your next step.
EndgameHints.effect_holdCorner: After {move}, your king stands on {to}. Keep checking the route to {corner} and the safety of any pawn capture.
EndgameHints.effect_supportedPawn: After {move}, your pawn on {to} is protected by your king on {king}.
EndgameHints.effect_pawnStep: After {move}, your pawn reaches {to}. The defender is still on {enemyKing}; check its next move before pushing again.
EndgameHints.effect_keySquare: After {move}, your king occupies {to}, one of the highlighted key squares for the pawn on {pawn}.
EndgameHints.effect_opposition: After {move}, your king on {to} faces the king on {enemyKing} across an empty square, with Black to move.
EndgameHints.effect_kingApproach: After {move}, your king stands on {to}, closer to the defender on {enemyKing}.
EndgameHints.effect_kingWall: After {move}, your king takes its post on {to}. Count the squares that your king and the rest of the team control near the defender.
EndgameHints.effect_knight: After {move}, the knight stands on {to}. Recheck how the whole team covers squares around {enemyKing}.
EndgameHints.effect_bishop: After {move}, the bishop uses the diagonal through {to}. Recheck how its colour coverage joins the other pieces.
EndgameHints.effect_restrict: After {move}, the defending king has {after} legal king moves instead of {before}. Keep building from that restriction.
EndgameHints.effect_checkFence: After {move}, the defender is in check and has {after} legal king moves. Your next plan depends on the reply.
EndgameHints.effect_keepFence: After {move}, the defending king has {after} legal king moves. This is a repositioning step; continue coordinating rather than expecting every move to be a check.
EndgameHints.covered: Your pieces now control these neighbouring squares around the defending king: {covered}.
